newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yield curve inverts further ahead of auction.
newsitem.headline: NZ yield curve inverts further ahead of auction.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.94 (PREV 92.94) 90-DAYS 7.38 (PREV 7.35)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.80 PCT (PREV 7.60) US 5-YR 6.15 (PREV 6.16)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 762.32 (PREV 763.87) Reuters NZ MCI -63 vs -61
New Zealand's yield curve steepened a notch on Thursday morning as the short end suffered from continuing looseness in the monetary index while bonds were supported by firmness in the U.S. market.
Bill dealers said the short end was completely in the command of the Trade-Weighted Index, which was down to 65.96 from 66.02 at Wednesday's close.
The Monetary Conditions Index at 762.32 was 13 points beyond the Reserve Bank's desired level and dealers said they are still wary of the bank making a statement.
However, one dealer said that the likelihood of a bank statement had lessened with June quarter CPI data less than a week away.
He said the risk was that the data will show inflation at less what the Reserve Bank has forecast which could legitimise conditions at more than 60 points easier than the RB's desired level.
The main event for the bond market today is the $300 million government bond tender including $150 million of a new benchmark bond maturing in 2009.

In theory the July 2009 bonds should go at around eight basis points above the 11/06s but dealers expect good demand for the new maturity, particularly from offshore players, and that could shrink the spread to nearer five points.
Higher cash and short bill rates were starting to cause pain for many players.
"It's bizare that we have a yield curve shaped this way with the economy in the situation it is," said one chief dealer.
"The question is, how far do interest rates have to go to attract interest in the kiwi?"
New Zealand short rates, at their highest since April, are now around 200 basis points above Australian rates.

"Looking at the relativities, you would think people would be looking to buy kiwi and sell aussie, (especially) on the uncertainties in the gold market with the aussie being a metals-driven currency."
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
